content: Female genital mutilation (FGM) has profound and detrimental effects on the health of women and their obstetric outcomes. Unlike male circumcision, FGM provides no medical benefits and causes significant harm to girls and women in numerous ways. Program managers and policymakers have an ethical responsibility to monitor and minimize potential harms arising from misunderstandings or misrepresentations of voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) for HIV prevention. Some of these harms may disproportionately affect women. Gender-related implications of male circumcision as an HIV prevention strategy include potential risk compensation, mischaracterization of the HIV risk-reduction effect of circumcision for men who have sex with men and transgender women, misrepresentation of the efficacy of circumcision in reducing sexual transmission of HIV from men to women, inadvertent promotion of unsafe sexual practices, and conflation of male circumcision with FGM. On the positive side, VMMC programming could provide opportunities to address harmful gender norms and gender-based violence. Research is needed to inform programming, service design, and delivery of VMMC for HIV prevention. This includes measuring the impact and contribution of VMMC within combination prevention services, assessing its effect on reducing other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and cervical cancer, understanding men’s values and preferences regarding HIV prevention, and evaluating the feasibility, cost, and effectiveness of expanding other services for men alongside VMMC. In many settings, VMMC for HIV prevention has been offered to younger adolescents aged 10–14 years. Decisions about providing VMMC to this age group must consider several factors within national and local contexts. These include the public health burden of HIV, the prevention effectiveness of VMMC, and the fact that circumcising boys in this age group in high HIV prevalence settings will avert future HIV and STI infections but not immediately if the individual is not yet sexually active. Adolescents’ capacity to provide informed consent varies, as their physical, emotional, and intellectual maturity evolves at different rates. Health care providers should aim to postpone non-emergency invasive and irreversible interventions until the child is sufficiently mature to provide informed consent. Laws or regulations should stipulate a minimum permissible age for consent to VMMC or refer to an assessment of the evolving capacity of the individual child. Supportive policies should be in place, and boys, parents, and health workers should receive adequate rights-based guidance on consent, assent, and confidentiality. VMMC services must ensure the lowest possible risk of adverse events. Limited evidence has shown differences in the type of serious adverse events (AEs) by adolescent age group, with a higher rate of certain rare serious AEs (such as glans injury and urethral fistula) in the 10–14-year age group compared to older adolescents. The precise magnitude of risk for these serious AEs among younger adolescents using the dorsal slit method is unknown but appears to be small (likely less than 1 per 100,000 VMMCs). Physical maturity is an important factor in the safety of VMMC in younger adolescents, and cognitive and psychosocial maturity are central to the capacity to provide informed consent. Adolescents with immature genitalia should defer VMMC until they are more physically developed. Male genital growth to near adult size is most often complete by 15 years. Adolescents who are not yet developed should be advised to return later when further advanced in puberty. The feasibility of offering some aspects of the VMMC package and other services, such as comprehensive sexuality education and internationally recommended vaccinations (e.g., tetanus toxoid-containing vaccination), at specific adolescent ages is unknown. Adolescents’, parents’, and communities’ preferences should be considered, including preferences for VMMC provided by the formal health sector rather than traditional practitioners. The three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that demonstrated the efficacy of VMMC for HIV prevention involved only males aged 15 years and older. No difference in the preventive effect is expected among younger adolescents, given early observations of the association of lower HIV risk with male circumcision in countries where infant circumcision is routine. However, no RCT evidence is available on the safety and acceptability of VMMC among younger adolescents, nor have studies focused on how to maintain effective coverage of VMMC, including among younger adolescents. Since 2007, informed consent standards regarding adolescents have been updated and need reconsideration. The 2007 recommendations emphasized scaling up access to male circumcision services for adolescents, young men, and older men at high risk of HIV, with involvement of the child in decision-making and the opportunity to provide assent or consent according to their evolving capacity. While males aged 10–14 years were not an initial priority population for VMMC, it has been estimated that annually, from 2015 through 2017, 42%–46% of VMMC uptake was among younger adolescents (10–14 years) and about 27% was among older adolescents (15–19 years) across 14 VMMC priority countries in East and Southern Africa. This represents a shift, particularly as countries reach higher coverage levels among adults, who were the priority group in the initial catch-up phase, and due to population demographics. Currently, one-quarter of the populations in these countries are young people, and that fraction will increase in the coming decade. To sustain effective HIV prevention coverage levels, programs need to reorient the delivery of services to uncircumcised cohorts of males. However, evidence on which age range to focus on has not been systematically considered, including information on safety for younger adolescents compared with older adolescents, approaches to maintaining high coverage levels for the lifelong benefit of HIV prevention, and integration or linkage with the delivery of other health interventions. Although there is extensive programmatic VMMC safety data, evidence systematically disaggregated by age is limited, including information on boys aged 10–14 years, who are at diverse stages in puberty. A systematic review identified only six publications with safety information specific to adolescent males (10–19 years) that were age-disaggregated in sufficient detail. Even in these studies, age groupings were diverse, and only two studies presented data specific to the younger age group of 10–14 years. Surveillance reports on serious AEs provided additional details, including data from PEPFAR’s Notifiable Adverse Events Reporting (NAER) surveillance system and ad hoc adverse event reports made to WHO.
